territorial_scope.description: Applies to any person who owns, operates or otherwise makes available an AI chatbot to individuals in the United States; the definition does not state where the person is located.

evidence.quote: any person who owns, operates, or otherwise makes available an artificial intelligence chatbot to individuals in the United States

summary.short: S. 3062 (GUARD Act, introduced 28 October 2025) would require any person who owns, operates or makes available an AI chatbot to individuals in the United States to verify users' ages, bar identified minors from AI companions, and make AI and non-professional disclosures. It also creates criminal offenses and civil penalties for chatbots that solicit minors or promote violence.
summary.long: S. 3062, the GUARD Act (introduced 28 October 2025), applies to any person who owns, operates or makes available an AI chatbot to individuals in the United States. Covered entities must require user accounts, verify users' ages with a reasonable age verification process (self-declaration and birth-date entry excluded), review verified accounts periodically, and limit, secure and delete age-verification data. Chatbots must disclose at each conversation start and every 30 minutes that they are AI, must not claim to be human when asked, must not represent themselves as licensed professionals, and must disclose they do not provide medical, legal, financial or psychological services. Covered entities must bar minors identified by age verification from AI companions. Section 4 makes it unlawful to design, develop or make available a chatbot knowing or with reckless disregard that it poses a risk of soliciting minors into sexually explicit conduct or of encouraging suicide, self-injury or violence; each offense carries a fine of up to $100,000. The Attorney General may seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, and state attorneys general may bring injunctive actions. The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment.

notes: Introduced text dated 28 Oct 2025, referred to Judiciary; no later version in the document. No other registry instrument is named. Internal points: criminal fines of up to $100,000 per offense (Sec. 4) and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation (Sec. 7(c)) are separate regimes. Sec. 3 definitions of chatbot and minor are repeated in new Sec. 91(a) with near-identical wording. Sec. 5(c)(1)(A) requires disclosure at 30-minute intervals; Sec. 5(c)(2)(B) requires 'reasonably regular intervals'. Sec. 7(e) is a savings clause for state laws at least as protective; it does not name a state instrument. Criminal offences in Sec. 4 are not assigned to a named enforcing authority.
